A no-hard-link file system moves fewer files, never others. The record is under home and replaced in one step. Each move is kept before it is made and dropped only after it is made or refused. back.lacking: How principle 1 holds at the old name. Taking away a name removes whatever is at that name at that moment. Between the hard link and its removal, another program (line 36's own example is a browser finishing a download) could put a new file at the old name, and the Mover would then delete that file. Undo has the same window at the kind-folder name. So the reason line 36 gives against a check made in advance applies just as much to the second step, and the lines do not say how that moment is closed. One way is to remove the name only if it still points to the linked file, which can still race. Another is a single system move that refuses a taken name, such as Linux renameat2 with RENAME_NOREPLACE or macOS renamex_np with RENAME_EXCL. Or the window can be accepted, with the why. The approver of the no-delete rule cannot tell which of these the Mover does.

chosen.why: With hard links only, a preview on FAT or exFAT shows moves that the move run then cannot make, so the old wording would contradict the Mover line (B-6). The new wording keeps the promise KR1.3 asks for: no move that differs from the preview.

chosen.chosen: The case of a file system without hard links goes in the existing line on moves the system refuses for another reason, not in a line of its own.
chosen.why: It is the same rule (leave the file in place, with the system's message), so one line holds it (B-7).

questions.question: Moving by a hard link and then taking away the old name still leaves a moment in which a file can be deleted. Between the two steps, another program, such as a browser finishing a download, can put a new file at the old name, and taking the old name away then deletes that new file. Undo has the same moment at the name in the kind folder. Python's standard library has no call that takes a name away only if it still points to a given file. Which should the Mover do? (a) Keep the hard link, and just before taking away the old name, check that it still points to the same file (same device and inode), leaving the file under both names if not; this narrows the moment to the gap between two system calls but does not close it. (b) Move each file by the system's own one-step rename that refuses a taken name, renameat2 with RENAME_NOREPLACE on Linux and renamex_np with RENAME_EXCL on macOS, called through ctypes from the standard library; there is no second step, so the moment is gone. Where the file system refuses this call, the file is left in place with the system's reason, as now. This replaces the hard-links-only decision, costs code for each system, and needs a trial first. (c) Keep the two steps as they are and state the moment in the architecture with why.
questions.recommended: (b), because a lost file is the one harm the UX puts first and (b) alone leaves no moment for it, while keeping the same behaviour of leaving files in place, with the system's reason, on file systems that refuse the call.
